attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter. He says this is his description of what the outcomes are.

semantics.note: It keeps his rejection of the 'efficacy leap' reading and his description of the outcomes. The core is a factual description of what hyperscaler AI pushes produce, and it is unquantified.

contract.note: The plain reading (tools work poorly and cost more time than they save, counting repeated use) is ordinary and fair. The projects are unidentified, 'half-functional' has no threshold, and the March window was chosen by the evaluator, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: A Microsoft self-report from March 2026 says employees report time savings. It is a company disclosure about selected cases, not independent or representative, and it does not cover the unidentified projects. At most it is a weak counterexample. It cannot meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a self-promotional company case study. It neither shows a representative picture of the described projects nor gives matched measurements of build hours against cumulative savings. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met, so the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: It captures both parts: no actual replacement, and layoffs caused by the cost of AI software. Dropping 'in practice not replacing anybody' is covered by the first clause.

contract.note: The budget crowd-out reading is a fair, ordinary reading. The 2025–March 2026 window is chosen by the evaluator, and it is unclear whether the claim covers all layoffs or the dominant mechanism, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Atlassian (a company disclosure) cut jobs to self-fund AI investment, which partly fits the claimed mechanism. But this is broader AI investment, not the cost of replacement tooling, and it also says AI reduces the roles needed in some areas. The item is mixed and indirect.

Secondary report of Block's stated efficiency rationale. This is a stated motive, not verified replacement of the work and not evidence about costs. It also covers the whole workforce, not engineers specifically.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only employer statements of motive. There are no records linking spending on AI tools to engineering layoffs, and none on who later did the eliminated work. The evidence neither establishes nor rejects the industry-wide causal claim.

attribution.note: He reports Mortenson's claim, but the forecast that it 'won't' happen is Zitron's own, firmly stated.

semantics.note: 'Obviously, blatantly won't' is an unhedged forecast that the whole project will not be complete by October 2026.

contract.note: All eight buildings finished and energized, with a deadline of October 31, 2026, is an ordinary reading of 'entire project completed by October 2026'.

evidence.note: Oracle's September 10 remarks (a company disclosure via transcript) say six of eight buildings had been delivered. This is a progress snapshot before the deadline and shows neither completion nor failure by October 31.

reviews.rationale: The deadline (October 31, 2026) falls after the evaluation date (October 28). Neither early-resolution trigger occurred: no verified completion of all eight buildings and no irreversible cancellation. Unfinished work before the deadline is not conclusive, so the forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: Verbatim, keeping 'wholly' and 'or even just maintain'. It is a claim of causal dependence, with a rhetorical edge ('convince people this is somehow rational').

contract.note: Reading 'wholly' as necessary dependence is fair. But the revenue baseline (fiscal Q4 2026) and how 'years into the future' is operationalised are the evaluator's choices, so interpretation does affect the result, despite the contract's flag.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's March 2026 announcement gives a deployment target about a year out. It shows advance planning, but not multiyear sales or revenue dependence.

OpenAI's September 2025 disclosure, which predates the claim, says Abilene workloads were already running. One prompt deployment says nothing about how much NVIDIA's total revenue depends on advance purchases.

reviews.rationale: No records link NVIDIA's revenue to the gap between purchase and deployment, or show what revenue would remain without multiyear advance purchases. Both items are company disclosures that bear only indirectly on this. The evidence does not establish or refute the claim that the dependence is total.
